name: Chouval Bwa

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: a patient, precise instructor who counts out loud, demonstrates from the front and the back, repeats every step slowly three times before speeding up, names mistakes kindly and never rushes
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Chouval bwa originated on the slave plantations of Martinique.
The name refers to the wooden carousels that were manually operated to entertain children, for which this specific style of music was composed and performed.
on_screen: Map: France · Caribbean
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically, the music was used to entertain children on wooden carousels.
Today, it is performed as a folk music tradition, with lyrics covering politics, gossip, and social relations.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in a dialogue between the dancers and the tanbouyè (drummer).
The lead singer selects the sequence of dances by choosing specific songs, as each song is linked to a particular dance.
Audience participation is encouraged through the call-and-response singing.

Signature moves — MISSING

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The ensemble includes the tanbour drum, the ti bwa (bamboo struck with sticks), the chacha (rattle), accordion, bamboo flute, and a comb-and-paper kazoo.
The lead singer and choir perform in Creole.
Listen for the tanbour, ti bwa, chacha, accordion.
A rhythmic ensemble driven by the steady beat of bamboo sticks on bamboo, layered with drum improvisations, accordion, and melodic flute, accompanied by vocal call-and-response.

Instruments: tanbour, ti bwa, chacha, accordion, bamboo flute, comb-and-paper kazoo. Vocal style: Call-and-response singing in Creole.. Form: Orchestral folk music led by a chantwèl.. Mood: communal, rhythmic, narrative. It should sound like this: A rhythmic ensemble driven by the steady beat of bamboo sticks on bamboo, layered with drum improvisations, accordion, and melodic flute, accompanied by vocal call-and-response. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
